papers.title: Spontaneous Hemodynamic Oscillations during Sleep Coordinate Directional CSF Flow in the Subarachnoid Space and Ventricles
papers.abstract: During sleep, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow is enhanced and thought to facilitate clearance of metabolic waste from the brain. Human imaging has shown that sleep is associated with large waves of bulk CSF flow in the fourth ventricle; however, the CSF flow dynamics around brain tissue are unknown. Here, we investigated how CSF flow is organized across the subarachnoid space, a key site both for fluid exchange across cortical surface and for transport out of the cranium. We used an MRI technology at 7 Tesla that simultaneously measures cortical hemodynamics and slow subarachnoid CSF flow and applied this during sleep. We found that spontaneous infraslow hemodynamic oscillations were coupled to spatially structured, directional CSF flow throughout both ventricular and subarachnoid compartments. Hemodynamic oscillations and fourth-ventricle bulk flow were both associated with brain-wide CSF flow at different phases, indicating that they reflect a single coordinated CSF movement cycle. Compared to cardiac pulsations, a canonical driver of CSF movement, hemodynamic-driven CSF flow showed a distinct directional pattern and was smaller in instantaneous amplitude but produced substantially greater cumulative displacement and thus greater potential for transport within an oscillation period. Together, these findings show that hemodynamic oscillations during sleep are coupled to temporally coordinated and directional CSF flow throughout the ventricles and subarachnoid space, suggesting that sleep-dependent neuronal activity drives fluid movement across the human brain in a distinct spatial pattern.

papers.title: Human Hippocampal Theta-Gamma Phase-Amplitude Coupling Signals the Distance to Remembered Goals
papers.abstract: In mammals, flexible navigation is believed to rely on a cognitive map of known locations supported by the hippocampus and surrounding medial temporal lobe structures. Hippocampal place cells typically exhibit spatial firing fields within a given environment. Moreover, their firing is modulated by the movement-related theta rhythm such that "theta sweeps" of place cell activity encode the trajectory towards a hidden reward location during goal-directed navigation. Here, we attempted to detect signatures of theta sweeps in the human hippocampal local field potential (LFP) recorded with intracranial EEG. Specifically, we hypothesised that sequences of locations along a planned trajectory encoded by distinct cell assemblies are associated with gamma activity at successive theta phases. To test this hypothesis, we asked N=9 patients with epilepsy to perform a spatial navigation task in desktop virtual reality while we recorded LFP signals from depth electrode contacts implanted across the medial temporal lobe. Consistent with our predictions, we found an increase in hippocampal theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling, a decrease in gamma power, and theta phase precession of gamma activity as hidden goal locations were approached and the sequence of locations remaining to be traversed became shorter. This suggests that goal-directed hippocampal theta sweeps during navigation are reflected in LFP theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling, and that these neural mechanisms of model-based planning are conserved across species.

papers.title: Probing the neural geometry of conscious object perception in time
papers.abstract: Conscious object recognition is a critical brain function, key to making sense of the plethora of visual inputs and guiding adaptive behavior. Yet, the sequence of neural processing underlying conscious object recognition remains unclear. Existing proposals alternatively suggest that conscious object recognition proceeds in a "coarse-to-fine" sequence or a "fine-to-coarse" sequence. Here, we recorded high-density EEG while participants of both sexes performed a threshold-level object recognition task under different viewing conditions. Both superordinate and basic-level category information emerged early in neural activity, followed by a late superordinate category representation in an abstract format that is disentangled from low-level object features. Strikingly, in the early period, while basic-level category information positively correlated with perceptual awareness, superordinate category information negatively predicted perceptual awareness. By contrast, both superordinate and basic-level category information positively correlated with objective categorization accuracy in the early period. In the late period, both levels of category information positively correlated with awareness. These results suggest that neural processing underlying conscious object perception proceeds from the basic to the superordinate category level.

papers.title: A KaiA Conformational Switch Links Day-Night Transitions to Clock Robustness
papers.abstract: Biological clocks require mechanisms that enable transition between temporal phases and buffer against environmental fluctuations. In the cyanobacterial KaiABC-based circadian oscillator, KaiA has been regarded as a daytime activator that is passively sequestered at night. Here we define KaiA as a conformationally regulated activator and an active catalyst of the night-to-dawn transition. We identify a single linker helix, 5, that acts as a structural switch, mediating a domain-driven "tug-of-war" that sets the open-closed equilibrium in KaiA. Structure-guided mutations that shift this balance in either direction abolish stable rhythmicity both in vitro and in cells. Also, we show that substoichiometric KaiA dismantles nighttime KaiB-KaiC complexes through interactions with the KaiC C-terminal tails and likely initiates an autocatalytic feedback loop that resets the phosphorylation cycle at dawn. Furthermore, we present two independent kinetic models that offer distinct, deterministic explanations for the clock's low-temperature amplitude decline and failure at 20 {degrees} C.

papers.title: Neural dynamics of induced throat vibrations during vocal emotion recognition
papers.abstract: Despite a large literature on the psychological and brain mechanisms of emotional prosody perception, the perspective of embodied cognition on these mechanisms has been largely neglected. Here we investigated the influence of induced bodily vibrations near the vocal tract on the categorization of emotionally ambiguous vocalizations while acquiring event-related potentials (ERPs) through electroencephalography. Emotional voices were morphed between a fearful expression and the speakers identity-matching angry expression, creating blends of emotions in each voice. In line with our hypotheses, behavioral results revealed that induced vibrations biased the participants emotion categorizations. Namely, induced throat vibrations of anger shifted responses toward anger for the most ambiguous voices, while fear vibrations shifted responses toward fear for anger-leaning voices. ERPs indicated that both anger and fear vibrations modulated frontocentral amplitude from about 75 ms, with the sign of the effect depending on time bins and morphing levels. These modulations show that vibrations are registered from early stages of processing. Source reconstruction highlighted effects of vibration types in prefrontal, cingulate, parietal, and medial and lateral temporal cortices, and to a lesser extent in somatosensory and insular cortices. Our results suggest that voice-associated vibrations may contribute to vocal emotion processing through an embodied feedback mechanism.

papers.title: Stimulus overlap confounds generalization in EEG foundation-model benchmarks
papers.abstract: Neural decoding benchmarks commonly evaluate generalization across participants while reusing the same experimental stimuli in training and test sets. This design cannot distinguish transfer to new stimuli from recognition of familiar material, a distinction that is increasingly important for electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models, pretrained models designed to learn reusable neural representations. Here we introduce a training-matched audit that varies stimulus overlap while holding test trials, training participants and stimulus counts fixed. Across ten tasks from seven EEG emotion datasets, stimulus overlap increased differential-entropy decoding accuracy in every task and accounted for 77% of above-chance seen-stimulus performance on FACED-9. Across representations, overlap-dependent gains tracked stimulus identifiability; for CBraMod and LaBraM, advantages over input-matched handcrafted features were concentrated on familiar stimuli. Architecture-matched random controls nevertheless showed transferable benefits of pretraining on unseen stimuli. These results separate participant generalization from stimulus generalization and provide a framework for evaluating both in neural decoding benchmarks.

papers.title: Membrane proteomics of the Drosophila circadian neural network
papers.abstract: The Drosophila brain contains approximately 240 pacemaker neurons that control circadian behaviors. Their molecular clocks are synchronized, but the phase of their rhythmic activity differs, so that specific groups of clock neurons can properly time various behaviors. To understand in depth how the circadian neural network functions, we surveyed its membrane proteome in the morning and evening, using in situ protein labeling coupled with mass spectrometry. We detected known regulators of circadian behavior and identified novel membrane or membrane-associated proteins in clock neurons. Through genetic screens, we found that many of these proteins regulate circadian behavior. In particular, Oct{beta}1R modulates evening locomotion under long photoperiod, while Piezo regulates morning activity under short photoperiod. Loss of Piezo alters rhythmic neuronal activity and compromises the structural plasticity of the neurons controlling locomotion at dawn. Our work thus illustrates the power of proteome-guided genetic screening to understand the mechanisms underlying circadian behavior.

papers.title: Goal-directed action selection relies on conjunctive representations that bind goals, actions and expected sensory outcomes
papers.abstract: Goal directed actions are performed to obtain specific sensory outcomes. However, theories of action control differ in how the brain encodes action-outcome predictions and whether they are encoded as separable components or integrated into conjunctive representations that support behavior and learning. Here, we tested whether predicted sensory outcomes are integrated into the neural representations underlying the selection of goal directed actions. Participants learned novel action-outcome contingencies and selected actions to generate specific sensory outcomes, while their brain activity was recorded using EEG. Combining time resolved multivariate decoding with representational similarity analysis, we tracked both feature specific and conjunctive neural representations over time. We found that expected sensory outcomes were integrated into high-dimensional conjunctive representations that could not be explained by a linear addition of individual features. The strength of these representations predicted trial to trial reaction times, alongside compositional action representations. Over time, the strength of compositional feature representations weakened, suggesting that the brain more selectively relied on conjunctive representations over the course of learning. These results provide neural evidence that predicted sensory outcomes are incorporated into behaviorally relevant conjunctive representations during action selection, consistent with theories that propose integrated action-outcome representations.

papers.title: Excitation-contraction coupling plasticity is revealed upon RyR2 depletion in adult mouse ventricular myocytes
papers.abstract: Ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2) is central to cardiac excitation-contraction coupling (ECC), translating electrical signals into sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca2+ release and mechanical contraction. Although constitutive deletion of RyR2 is lethal, adult hearts can withstand a significant reduction in RyR2 expression without overt ECC dysfunction. We hypothesized that ECC possesses intrinsic homeostatic plasticity that rapidly adapts to acute RyR2 loss to maintain cardiac performance. Using an adult tamoxifen-inducible RyR2 conditional knockout (RyR2cKO) mouse model, we evaluated cardiac structure, electrophysiology, and intracellular Ca2+ dynamics. RyR2cKO mice survived for weeks with <10% residual RyR2 protein expression. In vivo echocardiography and electrocardiography revealed normal cardiac structure and function. Confocal Ca2+ imaging in intact hearts and isolated ventricular myocytes showed preserved Ca2+ transient (CaT) amplitude but slower release kinetics and elevated SR load. Simultaneous patch-clamp and confocal Ca2+ imaging established that L-type Ca2+ current (ICa) and ECC gain were maintained in RyR2cKO myocytes. Expression of CaV1.2, NCX, and phospholamban remained unchanged, whereas SERCA2a, IP3 receptor, and VMP1 levels decreased. Pharmacological inhibition of IP3 receptors did not suppress CaT, ruling out alternative SR channel compensation. These findings reveal remarkable intrinsic ECC plasticity, where high RyR2 channel reserve, elevated SR Ca2+ load, and CaT autoregulation collectively maintain cardiac Ca2+ cycling and contractile function despite profound RyR2 depletion.

papers.title: One night of sleep deprivation reduces spatially patterned human brain clearance: implications for simulated tau propagation
papers.abstract: Neurotoxic protein fragments such as amyloid-beta and tau accumulate in characteristic staging patterns in Alzheimer's disease. The brain clears such substances via multiple systems, including the extracellular-extravascular route known as glymphatic clearance, but how such clearance is distributed across the brain, how this distribution is affected by sleep, and its implications for neurodegenerative disease progression remain unclear. Using Bayesian inference to fit a kinetic model of enhancement and clearance to longitudinal CSF tracer-enhanced MRI, we estimate CSF tracer clearance rates for every connectome region in 21 subjects. We find that clearance is spatially patterned across the living human brain and consistent between subjects. Clearance rates are amongst the highest in the entorhinal cortex and decrease across regions in Braak stage order. One night of sleep deprivation reduces mean clearance levels while leaving the spatial pattern largely unchanged. To study how mean clearance level and spatial pattern affect tau propagation in silico, we use the CSF tracer clearance rates as a proxy for regional tau clearance in a computational model of protein accumulation, spread, and regional damage. Across subject-specific simulations, clearance level and spatial pattern have distinct effects on tau propagation. The clearance level determines the timescale of simulated pathology, while the spatial pattern shapes its accumulation and onset. These results identify CSF tracer clearance as a spatially organised property of the human brain that is reduced by sleep deprivation, and suggest that its overall level and regional organisation may independently shape the timing and spatial progression of neurodegenerative proteinopathy.

papers.title: AMPK-dependent brain-wide norepinephrine release promotes recovery from metabolic coma in mice
papers.abstract: Coma is a pathological brain state characterized by loss of consciousness. How the brain recovers from coma remains largely unknown. Using mouse models of metabolic coma, we identified an endogenous neuromodulatory pathway that actively promotes coma recovery. In mice subjected to hypoglycemic coma, hypoglycemia triggered AMPK-dependent excitation of nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) neurons, which activated locus coeruleus (LC) norepinephrine neurons through a glutamatergic NTS-LC circuit. LC activation drives widespread norepinephrine release across cortical and subcortical regions, thereby promoting post-coma arousal. Notably, coma-associated brain-wide norepinephrine release was unconventional in both scale and duration, with a magnitude approximately 10-fold higher than physiological norepinephrine release during sleep-wake cycles. This neuromodulatory process also operated during hypercapnic coma. Vagus nerve stimulation accelerated coma recovery by engaging this endogenous anti-coma mechanism. Our findings uncover an AMPK-dependent brainstem circuit that actively restores arousal from metabolic coma, revealing a neural defense strategy against profound metabolic stress.

papers.title: Predictive Grid Cell Coding Does Not Require Explicit Planning
papers.abstract: Predictive grid cells, a recently discovered functional class of neurons in medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), exhibit grid-like tuning, not with respect to where an animal currently is, but where it will be. Such coding, which is disjoint from standard grid cell coding, appears consistent with the hypothesis that MEC supports predictive computations for goal-directed navigation. However, given that existing predictive coding theories have been used to understand standard grid cells, it remains unclear what the functional significance of predictive grid cells is. Furthermore, the extent to which predictive grid cells are generally present in MEC is unknown. To address these open questions, we analyze data from rodent electrophysiology recordings and recurrent neural networks (RNNs). In an independent, previously recorded MEC dataset, we find evidence of predictive grid cell coding when the animal is awake and exploring an open field environment, suggesting that they are a general feature of rodent MEC. In RNNs trained to path-integrate, which have previously been shown to develop units with grid-like representations, we also find units with predictive grid-like representations, even though the RNNs are not trained with a predictive objective. We validate the predictive grid tuning of these units by finding that they exhibit significant future path-dependence, even when controlling for the same allocentric spatial position. In addition, we find that band-like units, which have been found to play an important role in maintaining path-integration in the RNNs, exhibit greater predictive grid tuning than expected by chance. These results lead us to hypothesize that predictive grid cells are a property of the underlying grid cell circuit. We test this by looking for signatures of predictive grid coding in the MEC electrophysiological data collected during sleep, finding evidence in one recording. Collectively, our results challenge the idea that predictive grid cells must necessarily be used for explicit prediction and planning, and instead may be involved in shaping the population level activity of grid cells.

papers.title: Aging effects on retrospective and naturalistic encoding of time and their relationship with memory.
papers.abstract: In everyday life, attention is not explicitly directed toward time. Yet, we can reconstruct how long an experience lasted from the memory traces it left behind, a process intertwined with episodic memory and subjective experience. As both memory and temporal processing change with advancing age, investigating aging effects could provide critical insights on these reconstructive processes. In this study, 31 younger (aged 24{+/-}3) and 36 older (aged 69{+/-}6) healthy adults completed two EEG sessions: 1) a resting-state recording followed by an unexpected retrospective time estimation, and 2) a video-based prospective duration estimation task where participants encoded and judged the duration of 50 naturalistic videos (2-32s) varying in eventfulness. Using a cycle-by-cycle burst analysis of alpha (: 8-12 Hz), we examined oscillatory correlates of both retrospective temporal judgement and prospective temporal processing. Behaviorally, both groups reconstructed short intervals similarly, but older adults produced longer prospective duration estimates than younger adults for longer video clips (16-32s), particularly under low-eventfulness. Regression analyses also showed that individual differences in older adults' prospective duration judgments were influenced by both their retrospective time estimation and episodic memory abilities, especially for longer videos. At the neural level, resting-state -burst dynamics were higher in older adults and predicted, with -power, longer retrospective estimates in older adults. Additionally, resting-state -burst activity predicted -burst during video encoding in both groups. Together, these findings reveal that individual -power and -burst dynamics could constitute memory-based time-tracking mechanism that aging reshapes in ways that manifest behaviorally under naturalistic conditions.

papers.title: Convergent and Distinct Transcriptional Signatures in Suicide, Bipolar Disorder, and Major Depressive Disorder
papers.abstract: Globally, a person dies by suicide every 40 seconds, underscoring a major global public health concern. In the United States, suicide is the second leading cause of death among individuals aged 10-34 years. Suicide is a complex, multifactorial phenomenon influenced by genetic and epigenetic factors and is strongly associated with mood disorders, particularly major depressive disorder (MDD) and bipolar disorder (BD). However, the extent to which their molecular signatures converge or diverge across disorders and brain regions remains incompletely understood. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic literature review of suicide, MDD, and BD transcriptomic studies in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science. Eligible studies used human postmortem brain tissue, reported a complete genome-wide transcriptomic list of differentially expressed genes (DEG), and compared suicide decedents with psychiatric non-suicide individuals diagnosed with the same underlying disorder. Regarding BD, studies comparing affected individuals to unaffected controls were included. Single-cell and peripheral-blood studies were excluded because unavailable for suicide. Curated suicide and BD DEG datasets were integrated with a published bulk transcriptomic dataset of MDD. We identified both shared and disease-specific molecular signatures across suicide, BD, and MDD, and identified DEGs shared across brain regions and those that were region-specific. A total of 276 genes were shared across all three conditions, implicating cellular stress, hypoxia (VEGFA, ADM, NDRG1, DDIT4), immune and inflammatory signaling through TNF/NF-{kappa}B (IL1B, ICAM1, NFE2L2) and IL6-JAK-STAT3 pathways (STAT3, SOCS3, IL1R1m OSMR), complement activation (CIR, SERPiNA1, LGALS3), extracellular matrix remodeling (COL4A1, SERPINH1, PLOD2), and unfolded protein response (BAG3, WFS1, MTHFD2). Suicide-associated DEGs were prominently downregulated, and involved metal-ion homeostasis, stress responses, synaptic regulation, and circadian pathways, whereas BD showed downregulation in synaptic and vesicle-related processes alongside region-specific metabolic dysregulation. MDD exhibited changes in RNA processing, ribosomal function, and protein synthesis. Genetic integration revealed that 133 genes shared between BD and MDD had gene variants associated with the corresponding condition per GWAS. Transcription factor analysis identified 20 regulatory factors with altered activity across all three conditions despite differences in their predicted downstream targets. Overall, these findings suggest that suicide, MDD, and BD share aspects of their molecular and regulatory pathophysiology while exhibiting distinct patterns, including in a region-specific manner.

papers.title: Disease progression shapes circadian and locomotor disruption in a model of multiple sclerosis
papers.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system featuring a wide range of debilitating symptoms. Wearable activity recording devices have recently been adopted to improve symptom monitoring in MS, capturing symptoms related to sleep/wake cycles, circadian disruption, and fatigue. However, comparable measures of activity have yet been established in pre-clinical models of MS, the most widely used being experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). We therefore sought to characterize changes in continual home-cage activity over the course of EAE, and establish whether home-cage monitoring can be used as an observer-independent measure of disease progression. Our results showed that locomotor activity in the mid-active/dark phase was most severely affected by EAE. Disrupted circadian (24-hour) activity was observed during the peak and onset stages of disease. Bout activity analysis revealed >40-minute long activity bouts as a sensitive indicator of non-motor symptoms independent of clinical score-based motor deficits. Current assessment of disease progression in EAE relies on clinical scores, which primarily assess motor deficits through visual observation prone to observer bias. Various computed activity parameters were found to be altered during key disease stages, suggesting that a combination of activity measures can serve as objective indicators of disease progression. Overall, our results show that home-cage activity effectively captures signs of non-motor symptoms in the EAE model of MS and can serve as an observer-independent measure of EAE disease progression.

papers.title: Agency and Embodiment Provide Dissociable Benefits to Perception, Metacognition and Neural Processing During Active Sensing
papers.abstract: Metacognition, judging how reliable our own perceptual decisions are, is central to adaptive behavior. Such judgments hinge on the reliability of the sensory evidence on which that decision is based, and active sensing through self-directed exploration is known to improve perception itself. Yet, how agency, the authorship over self-initiated actions, and the processing of the sensory consequences, which is implicit to active sensing, modulate metacognition and its calibration, remains unknown. Whether physical embodiment adds to this beyond virtual exploration is similarly unclear, yet relevant both for daily life and for self-monitoring in agentic AI. Here, we combined a naturalistic auditory search paradigm with mobile electroencephalography. Twenty participants performed a target-detection task under three conditions: active embodied exploration , active screen-based exploration, and passive listening to replays of their own trials, while we obtained steady-state auditory evoked potentials (SSAEPs) to characterize stimulus-locked neural responses. We find that both agency conditions improved accuracy, metacognitive sensitivity, and overall SSAEP amplitude relative to passive listening, indicating that agency, rather than whole-body movement, drives these enhancements. Crucially, however, embodiment uniquely grounded both the target-evoked neural response and the subjects' confidence to immediate sensory evidence. Thus, agency alone broadly enhances perceptual and neural processing, but embodiment specifically anchors confidence, neurally and behaviorally, to the present.

papers.title: Coupled neuro-fluid dynamics in human bioelectromagnetism
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) are widely interpreted as direct, non-invasive measures of neural population activity, assuming surrounding tissue and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) act as passive volume conductors that distorts but do not contribute to signal generation. Using conductive-fluid phantom experiments, structural magnetic resonance imaging, and in vivo EEG and MEG recordings, the present report challenges this assumption. Mechanically driven conductive fluid generated structured, oscillatory, source-localizable electromagnetic signals resembling M/EEG in the absence of neural tissue, and interindividual differences in CSF volume systematically moderated M/EEG signal amplitude. These findings suggest that, at the scales accessed by invasive and non-invasive electrophysiology, electromagnetic and mechanical processes form a coupled system in which contributions of neural currents and fluid motion cannot readily be uniquely separated.

papers.title: A Benchmark of Unsupervised Circadian Phase Inference Methods for Bulk Transcriptomic Data
papers.abstract: Circadian phase can be inferred from gene expression when sample collection times are unavailable, but the available methods have not been systematically compared. We compared ten unsupervised phase inference methods and two clock-gene baselines on 25 datasets with reference times (16 real datasets from five studies and 9 simulations). The primary measure was the aligned circular mean absolute error (MAE), with a permutation test for significance, circular correlations and gene-level reconstruction of rhythmicity, acrophase and amplitude were secondary outcomes. CHIRAL had the lowest mean MAE (1.80 h, 95% confidence interval 1.21-2.97 h from resampling study families). The two clock-gene baselines (2.15 and 2.20 h) were next, followed by TEMPO, CYCLOPS and CYCLOPS 2.0 (2.49-2.80 h), and the confidence intervals of these six overlapped substantially. The other six methods had mean errors of 3.91-4.86 h, compared with 5.08-5.23 h for permuted phases. Accuracy depended on the dataset and on the strength of clock-gene rhythms, and, for several methods, on the random seed and the adjustment for batch or covariates. When the inferred phases were used to analyse gene rhythms in 22 datasets, the four leading methods identified rhythmic genes with a median ROC AUC of 0.64-0.70 and recovered gene acrophases with a median error of 0.18-0.64 h. In two mouse datasets without collection times, agreement with external reference acrophases differed between methods and tissues.
